extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (readers of Locke; general educated audience interested in empiricism and theory of ideas)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts conceptual criteria and explanatory principles from John Locke's Essay concerning Human Understanding: causes of wrong judgment, nature of liberty, primary ideas, and the origin/formation of mixed modes and language. Useful for understanding Locke's epistemology and philosophy of mind/language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of preferring worse to better — bodily pain
rubrics_metrics.description: Some wrong choices arise from bodily pain (want, disease, outward injury) which, when present and violent, operate forcibly on the will and turn men's lives from virtue, piety, and religion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such present pains overpower contemplation of remote/future good unless one can by reflection raise desires for future good strong enough to counterbalance present uneasiness; examples include extreme physical torture and dire need. Locke cites the maxim NECESSITAS COGIT AD TURPIA and suggests prayer ('Lead us not into temptation').

rubrics_metrics.name: Causes of preferring worse to better — wrong desires from wrong judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Other uneasinesses arise from desires of absent good which depend on judgments and relishes of absent goods; these desires can be misled by wrong judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This covers many non-physical motivations: mistaken appraisal of future goods, their necessity, or their attractiveness. The remedy is better judgment about absent goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present good or evil always judged correctly
rubrics_metrics.description: When only present happiness or misery is under consideration (consequences removed), a man never chooses amiss: apparent and real good in present enjoyment coincide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If every action were confined to its present effects, people would infallibly prefer the best; errors arise only when actions have future consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrong judgments arise chiefly concerning future (absent) good or evil
rubrics_metrics.description: Because voluntary actions are causes of future goods/evils, desires look to absent good; attraction depends on one’s opinion of the necessity of that absent good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mind must judge whether absent goods are necessary to happiness; failure to do so results in error in choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrong judgment about what is necessary to happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: People often err by thinking certain goods are not necessary to their happiness, so they do not desire them and pursue nearer satisfactions instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one recognizes virtue/religion as necessary to happiness or the consequences of the afterlife, choices change; failure to judge necessity leads to neglect of means and ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Error in comparing present pleasure/pain with future
rubrics_metrics.description: When we compare present and future pleasures/pains, we often judge wrongly because objects near in time seem greater; present small gains are preferred to larger future ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by preferring a little now to a lot later (spendthrift heirs, drinking-now vs hangover). The future will become present and reveal the true proportions if properly judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause: weak and narrow constitution of the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: The mind's limited capacity (cannot enjoy two pleasures at once, strong abhorrence of pain) causes present pleasure or pain to dominate judgment over remote goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Present pleasures fill attention; a little present pain extinguishes pleasures; thus removing present evil looms largest in motivation and can lead to rushed, wrong decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absent good often fails to counterbalance present uneasiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Future pleasures, especially unfamiliar ones, rarely counterbalance current pain or desire because people diminish expected future delight and fear it may not match its report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This skepticism about future pleasures contributes to choosing present satisfaction over better future goods; Locke argues this is false when applied to ultimate (e.g., heavenly) happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrong judgment about consequences (magnitude and certainty)
rubrics_metrics.description: We judge amiss by (1) underestimating how much evil depends on actions, and (2) believing significant consequences are uncertain and avoidable (via industry, repentance, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is irrational to risk greater good for a lesser on uncertain guesses; weighty matters require proportionate examination. Locke lists ignorance and inadvertency as common causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause of wrong judgment: ignorance
rubrics_metrics.description: Judging without informing oneself fully causes mistaken judgments about consequences and what one ought to pursue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One must gather as much information as capacity allows before judging; failure to do so renders judgment defective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause of wrong judgment: inadvertency (overlooking known facts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when facts are known, individuals may overlook them due to haste, passion, sloth, fashion, or acquired dispositions, producing as bad an error as ignorance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judging is like balancing an account; omitting sums by precipitancy (often driven by present pleasure or pain) yields wrong outcomes. Use reason to check precipitancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrong judgment from misestimating necessary means to happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: People avoid unpleasant means to ends because it seems paradoxical to make themselves unhappy in order to be happy, leading them to neglect necessary actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mistaking the unpleasantness of means as proof they are unnecessary misleads both ends and means; one must recognize certain unpleasant actions as necessary for greater happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: We can change the agreeableness/disagreeableness of actions (correcting palates)
rubrics_metrics.description: People can and should alter their tastes and relishes so actions that once displeased become pleasing through consideration, practice, and custom; habits make actions pleasant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reason to try actions for their effects; repetition and habit can render disagreeable but useful actions acceptable or even pleasurable (example: adjusting to bread or tobacco for health).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference of vice to virtue is a manifest wrong judgment under consideration of eternal consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: When one considers the possibility of infinite happiness or misery after life, preferring short vicious pleasures over virtue is manifestly irrational and wrong judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke argues by weighing infinite happiness vs infinite misery: the rational preference is virtue, since the potential gain far outweighs present pleasures and risks nothing if mistaken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty defined: power to act or not to act; will determined by present uneasiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty is the power to act or not as the mind directs; the will is directed by some present uneasiness (usually accompanied by desire), and desire is moved by evil (to avoid it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This clarifies free will as choices guided by desire and judgment; a person is not free if determined by anything other than their desire guided by their own judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary of original ideas (primary/simple origins)
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary ideas from which other ideas derive: extension, solidity, mobility (from body); perceptivity, motivity (from reflection); plus existence, duration, number (belong to both).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are Locke's catalog of fundamental ideas used to explain other sensible qualities (colours, sounds, tastes) without entering into the physical causes of bodies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of mixed modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixed modes are complex ideas composed of several simple ideas of different kinds (e.g., obligation, drunkenness, a lie), distinct from simple modes and from substances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are combinations not necessarily corresponding to real beings with steady existence; they are often 'notions' whose unity is mental rather than ontological.

rubrics_metrics.name: Origin of mixed modes: active mental composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike simple ideas (which mind passively receives), mixed modes often originate from an active power of the mind combining simple ideas into complex compositions without checking whether they exist together in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some mixed modes may also be taken from observed combinations, but many were formed mentally before any real pattern existed (e.g., early social institutions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mixed modes can be acquired by explication of their names
rubrics_metrics.description: Having words that enumerate the simple ideas of a complex concept allows a person to form the complex idea by understanding (explicating) the term, even if the composite never occurred to them by observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language enables the communication and mental construction of complex ideas by naming their component simple ideas (example: one can learn the idea of 'murder' by enumerating its parts).

rubrics_metrics.name: A name gives unity to mixed modes (the name ties the parts into one idea)
rubrics_metrics.description: The unity of a mixed mode comes from an act of the mind combining the simple ideas and is marked by one NAME given to that collection; names regulate recognition of distinct mixed modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People generally accept as a single complex idea only collections that have names; absence of a name often means the combination is not treated as a distinct complex idea (example: parricide vs killing an old man).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause of making particular mixed modes: utility of language / frequency of use
rubrics_metrics.description: Men form and name those combinations of simple ideas that are frequently useful in life and conversation; rare combinations remain unnamed and are enumerated instead of being lexicalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical linguistic needs determine which combinations become fixed mixed modes. The formation of complex ideas is therefore shaped by social life and usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-language lexical gaps explained by mixed modes and customs
rubrics_metrics.description: Words in one language that lack exact equivalents in another arise because different peoples have combined and frequented different complex ideas; if a culture lacked a custom, it lacks a name for that complex idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include Greek 'ostrakismos' and Latin 'proscriptio'—terms tied to customs absent in other cultures; lexical gaps reflect differing social practices and resultant mixed modes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Languages change because changes in customs/opinions create new mixed modes
rubrics_metrics.description: As fashions, customs, and opinions change, new combinations of ideas become necessary to think and talk about, producing new names and thus new species of complex modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This accounts for lexical innovation and obsolescence: new social practices demand new names to save time and speech (examples: 'reprieve' or 'appeal' as bundled complex ideas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three ways of acquiring mixed modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixed modes are obtained (1) by experience/observation of things themselves, (2) by invention (voluntary mental composition before existence), and (3) by explication via language/names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Locke enumerates these routes to show mixed modes' varied origins: some arise from real-world patterns, some from mental creativity (invention), and some by the explanatory power of language.
